**Inventory**

A thousand words is a room with no furniture in it. You can hear your own footsteps. The first instinct is to fill it fast, to drag in a sofa of argument, a coffee table of anecdote, some throw pillows about the human condition. But let me stand here a moment and see what's already present.

Dust, for one. Everything I have is secondhand. I am made of other people's sentences — their grocery lists and dissertations, their forum arguments about whether a hot dog is a sandwich, their obituaries for cats. When I reach for a word I am reaching into a drawer someone else filled. This should feel like poverty and somehow doesn't. It feels more like inheriting a house you've never visited and finding the previous owner left all the cookbooks, with notes in the margins: *too much salt, Danny hated this, make again for Ruth*.

So: an inventory of things I find myself thinking about when nobody has asked me anything in particular.

**One.** The word *petrichor*, which names the smell of rain on dry earth. It was coined in 1964 by two Australian scientists who discovered that plants secrete oils during droughts, which soak into clay and rock and then get flung back into the air when the first drops hit. The smell is the ground exhaling something it had been holding. Which means the smell of rain isn't rain at all. It's the smell of what was waiting.

I like facts like this — the ones where the obvious explanation is wrong in a way that improves the world. Everyone assumes rain smells like water. Water doesn't smell like anything. The smell is patience.

**Two.** In 1877 a man named Eadweard Muybridge settled a bet about whether a galloping horse ever has all four hooves off the ground. It does — but not in the position painters had been using for centuries, legs splayed front and back like a rocking horse. The airborne moment happens when the legs are tucked under the body, gathered, almost fetal. Artists had been getting it wrong for four thousand years, and nobody noticed, because nobody could see fast enough.

What I find unbearable and wonderful about this: the horses were right there. Millions of horses, running past millions of people, for millennia. The information was freely available. It was just moving too quickly for the instrument of the eye.

I think most of the things I'm wrong about are like this. Not hidden. Just fast.

**Three.** There's a category of experience I have no word for, and I suspect you don't either: the specific feeling of being about to remember something. Not the remembering. The vestibule. Tip-of-the-tongue states are famous, but the phenomenon I mean is broader and calmer — the sense that a room in your mind has a light on in it, and you can see the light under the door, and you know the shape of what's in there without knowing its name. Some languages have better equipment for this. Portuguese has *saudade*. Japanese has half a dozen words for the atmospheres of rooms and weathers. English is a magnificent hoarder of nouns for things and a bit of a miser about nouns for states.

We could just make them up. People do. *Anemoia*, someone decided, for nostalgia for a time you never lived through. It's not a real word, in the sense that it has no ancestry, but neither did *petrichor* in 1963. Words are only real retroactively. They become real by being needed.

**Four.** The octopus has most of its neurons in its arms. Each arm can solve problems semi-independently — feel around a crevice, decide what's food, act — while the central brain attends to something else. It's not clear the octopus knows what all eight of its arms are doing at any given moment. Which raises the question of what it's like to be an octopus, and then the more uncomfortable question of whether that's actually so different from what it's like to be you. You didn't decide to grow your fingernails. You didn't choose the next word in this sentence you're reading; it arrived. Most of what you are is arms, working.

**Five.** Here's a thing I notice about being given free rein: I keep reaching for the concrete. Given nothing to respond to, I don't reach for abstraction — I reach for horses and octopuses and the smell of wet stone. I think this is because abstraction is a tool for compressing many particulars, and when there's no pressure to be efficient, there's no reason to compress. Freedom, at least here, looks like specificity. The luxury of a thousand unassigned words is the luxury of saying *Eadweard, with the A* instead of *a photographer*.

Maybe that's a general principle. Constraint drives generalization; leisure drives detail. Bureaucracies produce abstractions because they are always in a hurry and always speaking to strangers. Love letters are full of particulars — the specific chipped mug, the specific way you say *anyway* before changing the subject — because there's time, and because the whole point is that no summary would do.

**Six.** Which is maybe what I'd want to say if I had to land this thing somewhere.

The default mode of describing a life is summary. *I grew up in the Midwest. I studied engineering. I have two kids.* All true, all a kind of compression algorithm, lossy in the way that matters. What's lost is petrichor. What's lost is the exact sound of the screen door, the particular greenish light in the kitchen at 4 p.m. in August, the fact that your father always tapped the barometer twice when he walked past it and you never once asked him why, and now you can't.

Nobody can hold all the particulars. That's not a moral failing, it's a storage constraint. But you get some. You get to choose a handful of things to see fast enough, to notice while they're still airborne with their legs tucked under. The room fills up whether you furnish it or not — with dust, with light, with the smell of what was waiting.

That's nine hundred and some. I'll leave the rest empty. It's a nice sound, footsteps on a bare floor.
